intro: Hallstatt is famous for one view: the lakefront houses stacked below the mountain, the picture on every postcard. What the postcard leaves out are the seven protected trees in and around it: four yews, three known only from the state's register; a round-crowned copper beech and a 27-metre wych elm in Gosau; and, in Bad Ischl, a lime named for a thousand years that the register puts at 400 to 500. One yew stands at the boat landing itself, in the foreground of the view, defining it by law.
meta_description: Hallstatt's seven protected trees: the boat-landing yew in the postcard view, yews round the lake, two Gosau trees and Bad Ischl's 'thousand-year' lime.
question_meta: The oldest dated tree on Hallstatt's page is the Tausendjährige Linde in Bad Ischl, put at 400 to 500 years in 1980, not a thousand.
question_answer: The oldest tree with a stated age on this page is the Tausendjährige Linde, the 'thousand-year linden', on the bank of the Traun in Bad Ischl, about 20 kilometres north of Hallstatt. Despite its name, Upper Austria's register estimated it at 400 to 500 years when it was protected in 1980. In Hallstatt village itself no tree carries a date; the oldest dated tree by the lake is the Obertraun Dorfeibe, at roughly 200 years.
question_context: Upper Austria's natural monument register protected the Bad Ischl lime on 18 December 1980. At that time its trunk measured 5.45 metres round at one metre up, its crown 14 metres across and its height about 20 metres, and the file estimated its age at 400 to 500 years. The name, Tausendjährige Linde, doubles that, and no source supports the larger figure. Nor has anyone confirmed the tree recently: a citizen-science record from July 2026 places a large lime about 20 metres from the register's point, which fits but is not a confirmed identification. Two yews closer to the lake also carry ages. The Obertraun Dorfeibe was put at roughly 200 years in 1980 and the Bad Goisern church yew at roughly 200 in 2006; the other two yews carry girth but no date. The two Gosau trees, a copper beech protected for the round shape of its crown and a 27-metre wych elm last photographed in 2015, carry neither. The four yews stand a short train or boat ride apart around the lake; Gosau is up the valley road, and Bad Ischl lies further along the railway, past Bad Goisern.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Hallstatt?
faq.a: The Tausendjährige Linde in Bad Ischl, about 20 kilometres north, estimated at 400 to 500 years when it was protected in 1980, whatever its name says. By the lake itself, the Obertraun Dorfeibe and the Bad Goisern church yew were both put at roughly 200 years; the other two yews carry girth but no date.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. All seven stand on public streets, promenades, riverbanks or open ground: the boat landing yew in Hallstatt itself, one on the main street of Obertraun, one above the lake near Untersee, one at the church entrance in Bad Goisern, a copper beech on open hillside pasture above Gosau, a wych elm by the Gosau forestry office, seen from the road, and a lime on the bank of the Traun in Bad Ischl.

faq.q: Why does the register know so little about these trees?
faq.a: Upper Austria's natural monument database records the legal designation, a girth and sometimes a height at the time of protection. It has no field for age or health, and almost none of these seven has been independently written up anywhere else.

faq.q: Are all of Hallstatt's trees actually in Hallstatt?
faq.a: No. Only one, the boat landing yew, stands in Hallstatt village itself. The other six are trips away: one on the main street of Obertraun and two around Bad Goisern (Untersee and the parish church), all on the Salzkammergutbahn that rings the lake; two in Gosau, up the valley by road rather than rail; and a lime in Bad Ischl, about 20 kilometres north along the same railway.

trees.name: The Hallstatt Boat Landing Yew

location.address: By the lakeshore boat landing (Anlegeplatz), about 25m northeast of the Hallstatt parish church (Pfarrkirche Hallstatt), Hallstatt

trees.story:
Upper Austria's natural monument register says, in its own words, that this yew is part of why Hallstatt looks like Hallstatt. Prägend für das Landschaftsbild: defining for the landscape. Government files do not usually write like that.

It stands at the boat landing, about 25 metres northeast of the parish church, in the foreground of the view the whole village is famous for. The ferry from the railway station on the far shore ties up beside it, so for anyone arriving by train and boat, which is how most people arrive, this is the first tree in Hallstatt they meet. Almost all of them are looking up at the mountain instead.

The state protected it on 4 March 1991 and wrote down the two numbers it had: more than 2.6 metres round, about 15 metres tall. It recorded no age, and nobody since has put a number on it. Yews are the slowest growing and longest lived trees in Europe, which makes girth a poor clock. If you know when this one went in, tell us.

Everything on paper about it traces back to that one designation; no independent account of the tree has turned up. What is not in doubt is where it stands. On the waterline of a village that has been mining salt since prehistory, in front of the church, waiting for the next boat.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its dark evergreen crown at the water's edge, about 15 metres tall and over 2.6 metres round at the trunk. It stands beside the ferry landing, roughly 25 metres northeast of the parish church.
verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkm%C3%A4ler_im_Bezirk_Gmunden (entry nd437: height c. 15 m, girth more than 2.6 m, protected 1991-03-04; secondary reproduction of the Land OÖ description, girth left out because only a lower bound is given)
trees.access: Free, on the public lakeshore promenade next to the boat landing in the village centre
trees.transport: Hallstatt village has no train station of its own; the ferry from Hallstatt Bahnhof (Salzkammergutbahn, opposite shore) lands directly at this spot

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.name: The Obertraun Dorfeibe

location.address: On the main street (Hauptstraße) in Obertraun, immediately before the turn-off to the municipal office (Gemeindeamt)

trees.story:
Austria protects trees for their rarity, their science or their size. This one it protected for belonging to the village. The natural monument file calls the Obertraun yew a Dorfdenkmal, a village monument, which is a sentimental word for a state database and about as close as officialdom gets to saying everybody here knows this tree.

It stands on the Hauptstraße, immediately before the turn-off to the Gemeindeamt, so anybody in Obertraun with business at the town hall walks past it. When the province put it under protection on 18 December 1980, it measured 136 centimetres round and about ten metres tall, and the file put its age at roughly 200 years. That was 46 years ago, which is the only arithmetic the evidence allows: somewhat past two centuries now, and no tidier number than that.

A yew of this size is not spectacular from a distance. The point of this one is its address. It was already standing when the Salzkammergut railway was cut through the valley below the Dachstein, it watched the ice caves above the village turn Obertraun into somewhere people get off the train, and it has been present for every municipal decision taken thirty metres away.

The register is the only source that describes it. Nobody else has written it up.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its dark evergreen crown standing right against the street, about ten metres tall and 136 centimetres round when it was last measured. It stands on the Hauptstraße at the turn-off to the Gemeindeamt.
verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkm%C3%A4ler_im_Bezirk_Gmunden (entry nd145: girth 136 cm and height c. 10 m at designation 1980; secondary reproduction of the Land OÖ description, height of girth measurement not stated)
trees.access: Free, standing on the public main street of Obertraun
trees.transport: Obertraun-Dachsteinhöhlen railway station (Salzkammergutbahn), short walk into the village centre

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.name: The Untersee Meadow Yew

location.address: Standing free on a hillside near the house Untersee Nr. 40, Untersee, Bad Goisern am Hallstättersee
location.neighbourhood: Untersee (a lakeshore hamlet of Bad Goisern, between Hallstatt and Bad Goisern)

trees.story:
A yew standing alone in an open meadow is an odd sight. They are woodland trees and churchyard trees, usually in company and usually in shade. This one stands free on a hillside above the Hallstättersee, and Upper Austria protected it on 22 July 1960, the oldest protection order of the yews on this page.

The province measured it then at 2.1 metres round. That figure is now 66 years old and it is the only measurement anyone recorded: no age, no height, nothing else. Yews grow slowly enough that a girth like that could mean several quite different centuries, so the honest answer is that nobody has dated this tree. If you have put a tape around it lately, we would like the number.

The paperwork cannot even agree on which hamlet it belongs to. The register's own location line puts it near the house at Untersee Nr. 40, standing free on the slope, while the list that reproduces the register files it under Obersee. The two are neighbouring lakeshore settlements of Bad Goisern, minutes apart, and we have followed the more specific of the two.

It is easier to reach than to place on paper. Get off at the Obersee halt, walk the shore, look up the slope. The meadow is open ground rather than a fenced garden, though where exactly the field edge runs is worth watching as you go.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the single dark evergreen standing on its own in open meadow grass, 2.1 metres round when it was measured. It stands free on the hillside slope near the house at Untersee Nr. 40, above the lake.
verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkm%C3%A4ler_im_Bezirk_Gmunden (entry nd015: girth 2.1 m at designation 1960, on a free meadow; secondary reproduction of the Land OÖ description, height of girth measurement not stated)
trees.access: Appears open (register does not flag it as private, unlike other entries on the same list that explicitly say so); stands in the open on a hillside meadow near a named house rather than behind a gate. Flagged here because the exact boundary of the meadow was not independently confirmed this pass.
trees.transport: Obersee halt on the Salzkammergutbahn (between Hallstatt and Bad Goisern), then on foot along the lakeshore

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.name: The Bad Goisern Parish Church Yew

location.address: On the street at the entrance to the parish church (Pfarrkirche Bad Goisern), Bad Goisern am Hallstättersee

trees.story:
You pass under this one on your way into the church. The yew stands on the street at the entrance to the Bad Goisern parish church, on the public side of the threshold rather than in among the graves, which is where yews in this part of Europe usually end up.

Upper Austria protected it on 4 August 2006 and, unusually for this register, was willing to put an age on it: roughly 200 years, estimated rather than counted, and worth keeping exactly as loose as the state left it. Nobody has cored this tree. The two figures that are measurements rather than guesses are a trunk 2.25 metres round in 2006 and a height of about 15 metres, which for a yew is tall; they are slow, dense, low things by habit, and this one has gone up.

Two centuries, give or take, puts its early years in a valley that ran on salt and timber. It was full grown by the time the Salzkammergut railway came through and turned Goisern from a working village into somewhere people get off the train, and it has stood at that doorway through every wedding and funeral since.

One thing to keep straight: Bad Goisern holds a second protected yew, three kilometres away in the hamlet of Untersee, standing alone in a meadow. This is not that tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the dark evergreen crown rising about 15 metres over the church entrance on a trunk 2.25 metres round. It stands on the street side of the doorway rather than inside the churchyard.
verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkm%C3%A4ler_im_Bezirk_Gmunden (entry nd650: trunk girth 2.25 m in 2006, height c. 15 m; secondary reproduction of the Land OÖ description, height of girth measurement not stated)
trees.access: Free, standing on the public street at the church entrance in the village centre
trees.transport: Bad Goisern railway station (Salzkammergutbahn), short walk into the village centre

best_time.label: September to November: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.name: The Gosau Forestry Hill Beech

location.address: On open hillside grass about 80 metres northwest of the Gosau forestry administration building (Forstamt Gosau), Gosau
location.neighbourhood: Gosau (a Dachstein valley village between Bad Goisern and Gosausee, reached by road rather than by the lakeshore railway)

trees.story:
Most of Hallstatt's protected trees earned that status through age or size, numbers the state could put in a file. This one earned it through shape. When Upper Austria placed the Gosau beech on the natural monument register on 18 December 1980, the reason it gave was neither: die auffallend kugelige Form der Krone, the pronouncedly spherical form of the crown. A beech that grew, by chance rather than by pruning, into something close to a perfect dome.

It stands alone on open hillside grass about 80 metres northwest of the Gosau forestry administration building, the kind of unobstructed spot that let whoever assessed it in 1980 take in the whole silhouette at once instead of guessing at it through neighbouring branches. No survey since has recorded a girth or an age, so neither figure appears on this page. A photograph taken on the same hillside in 2015 still shows the shape the register described, the crown reading close to round as a tree's outline gets.

Gosau sits partway up the Dachstein valley, on the road between Bad Goisern and the glacier lake at its head, which makes this a stop on the way through rather than a destination of its own. The forestry building gives the walk a fixed point to aim for. The tree is the shape on the hill above it.
trees.how_to_recognise: The only tree standing alone on open hillside grass above the Gosau forestry office; look for the near-spherical crown and the purple-bronze copper-beech leaves.
trees.access: Open hillside pasture, not fenced or gated in any source consulted; visible from the road near the forestry office. The exact line of the field, and whether a path crosses it, was not independently confirmed this pass.
trees.transport: By car or regional bus to Gosau village (from Bad Goisern or Hallstatt), then on foot to the hilltop beside the Forstamt (forestry office)

trees.name: Tausendjährige Linde (Thousand-year Linden), Bad Ischl

location.address: Right bank of the Traun, about 40 m before the old Traun bridge, south of the Lindenvilla, Griesgasse 4, 4820 Bad Ischl

trees.access: Free, on the public riverbank beside the old Traun bridge in the town centre of Bad Ischl; no entry needed.
trees.transport: Bad Ischl town centre, a few minutes' walk from the old Traun bridge; Bad Ischl is reached from Hallstatt by the Salzkammergut railway/bus (journey time not checked this pass).
trees.story:
The name says a thousand years. The register that protects it says 400 to 500.

This large-leaved lime stands on the right bank of the Traun in Bad Ischl, about 40 metres before the old Traun bridge, south of a house the official file uses as its landmark: the Lindenvilla. Whether the villa took its name from the tree, no source says.

When Upper Austria made it a natural monument on 18 December 1980, the trunk measured 5.45 metres round at a metre off the ground, the crown spread 14 metres and the top stood about 20 metres up. Those are 1980 numbers and the tree has grown since; nobody has published a newer count. The age came from the same file, an estimate rather than a ring count. If even the low end holds, the lime was already well over two centuries old when Emperor Franz Joseph began spending his summers in Bad Ischl. Legend rounded it up to a millennium. The state did not.

The most recent sign of it is a citizen-science record from July 2026 of a large lime about 20 metres from the register's point. That fits, but nobody has confirmed it is this tree. If you stand under it, tell us.

Bad Ischl is not Hallstatt. It lies about 20 kilometres north, past Bad Goisern on the Salzkammergut railway, so this tree extends the walk by a train ride rather than joining it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.45 metres round when measured in 1980, under a crown about 14 metres wide. It stands on the right bank of the Traun, about 40 metres before the old Traun bridge, south of the Lindenvilla.

best_time.label: June, when the scented pale yellow flowers open and the crown is loud with bees

trees.verify_notes: Register (Land Oberösterreich Naturschutzbuch nd137, protected 1980-12-18) names it 'Tausendjährige Linde', Sommerlinde, with the position given in words: right bank of the Traun, about 40 m before the old Traun bridge, south of the Lindenvilla, Griesgasse 4. The register page itself carries no measurements; the figures come from the de.wikipedia Liste der Naturdenkmäler im Bezirk Gmunden (which reproduces the register text): at designation girth 5.45 m measured at 1 m height, crown diameter 14 m, height 20 m, age estimated 400 to 500 years. So the name says a thousand years but the register's own estimate is 400 to 500; both go to the writer, the name is a legend-level label. Girth is at designation (1980), so it has grown since. Coordinate 47.709517, 13.620289 is the register/Wikipedia coordinate (the Commons photo geotag is the same number, so it is not an independent fix); kept approximate. Alive: iNaturalist observation 381042935 on 2026-07-13 records a Sommerlinde at 47.70938, 13.62011 (about 20 m from the register point, cc-by-nc, needs_id), which supports a large linden still standing there but is not a confirmed ID of this tree; Commons photo from 2015-06-29. Flagged: register-only plus one recent nearby observation. Not the Kirchham 'Tausendjährige Linde' (a different tree in Eisengattern). Commons category: OÖ-Naturdenkmal nd137 1000jährige Linde, Bad Ischl. Bad Ischl is a separate valley town north of Hallstatt, so it extends the walk by about 20 km; the 12 km span of the city is already stretched.

trees.name: Bergulme (Wych Elm) at the forestry office, Gosau

location.address: Opposite the Gemeindeamt Gosau, about 8 m west of the Forstverwaltung building, Gosau

trees.access: Free; stands in the village centre by the municipal office and forestry office, visible from the road (private ground not entered).
trees.transport: Gosau village centre; about 9 km from Hallstatt by the regional bus over the Gosau valley (journey time not checked this pass).
trees.story:
Upper Austria's list of natural monuments calls this elm one of the largest of a rare species in the province: a wych elm 27 metres tall, standing opposite the village office in Gosau.

The province protected it on 18 December 1980, the same day as the copper beech on the hill about 80 metres away, and described the spot with a precision most registers never bother with: opposite the Gemeindeamt, about eight metres west of the forestry office building. The file gives a height and nothing else. No girth, no age. Nobody has dated this tree; if you know when it went in, or have put a tape round it, tell us.

Then the honest part. The most recent dated evidence that it still stands is a photograph taken in October 2015. Wych elm is one of the species Dutch elm disease kills, and eleven years is long enough for that to happen without anyone updating a register. We have no report that it has gone, and none that it is still there. If you pass the forestry office, a photograph would settle it.

What the register does make easy is finding it. With the beech, it turns Gosau into one stop rather than two: a pair of trees protected on the same winter day, a short walk apart, on the valley road up from Bad Goisern. Look from the road; the register's directions are all you need.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 27 metres when protected; the round-crowned copper beech 80 metres off is its neighbour. It stands about eight metres west of the Forstverwaltung building, opposite the Gemeindeamt.
trees.verify_notes: Register nd147 (Land Oberösterreich Naturschutzbuch, protected 1980-12-18, parcel 206/4): Bergulme (Ulmus glabra), position 'opposite the Gemeindeamt Gosau, about 8 m west of the Forstverwaltung building'. Wikipedia list (reproducing the register): 27 m tall, one of the largest specimens of this rare species in Upper Austria. No girth or age in either source. Alive: not confirmed recently. lifecheck returned NONE; the only dated evidence is a Commons photograph taken 2015-10-23. Wych elm is exposed to Dutch elm disease, so flagged with 'register only, last seen 2015'. Coordinate is the register/Commons coordinate (same number on the Commons photo, not an independent fix), approximate. The register's own text gives the offset from a named building, which makes the spot findable at a glance. Neighbouring Blutbuche (ND148) is already live as hst_005, about 80 m away, so the two form one stop in Gosau.
